front: A subnet uses the CIDR prefix \(/26\). How many usable host addresses are available per subnet?
explanation: Host bits: \(32 - 26 = 6\). Total addresses per subnet: \(2^{6} = 64\). Exclude the network and broadcast addresses: \(64 - 2 = 62\) usable hosts.

front: A Class C network \(192.168.10.0/24\) is subnetted with a \(/28\) mask. How many subnets are created, and how many usable hosts does each subnet support?
explanation: Borrowed bits: \(28 - 24 = 4 \Rightarrow 2^{4} = 16\) subnets. Host bits: \(32 - 28 = 4 \Rightarrow 2^{4} - 2 = 14\) usable hosts per subnet.

front: A host is configured with IP address \(192.168.1.200\) and subnet mask \(255.255.255.192\) (\(/26\)). What is its network (subnet) address?
explanation: For \(/26\), the block size in the last octet is \(256 - 192 = 64\). Subnet boundaries are \(0, 64, 128, 192\). Since \(192 \le 200 \le 255\), the host lies in the block starting at \(192\), so the network address is \(192.168.1.192\).

front: A subnet has network address \(172.16.20.0\) with mask \(255.255.255.224\) (\(/27\)). What is the subnet's broadcast address?
explanation: For \(/27\), host bits \(= 5\) and block size \(= 2^{5} = 32\). The subnet spans \(172.16.20.0\) through \(172.16.20.31\). The broadcast address is the last address in the block: \(172.16.20.31\).

front: A single subnet must accommodate at least \(500\) hosts. What is the smallest subnet (longest prefix) in CIDR notation that satisfies this requirement?
Express the subnet mask \(255.255.255.240\) in CIDR (slash) prefix notation.
explanation: Each \(255\) octet contributes \(8\) one-bits: \(3 \times 8 = 24\). The last octet \(240 = 11110000_{2}\) contributes \(4\) one-bits. Total \(= 24 + 4 = 28\), so the mask is \(/28\).

front: A \(1500\)-byte packet is sent over a link of bandwidth \(10\ \text{Mbps}\). Neglecting propagation delay, find the transmission (serialization) delay.
explanation: Packet size in bits: \(1500 \times 8 = 12{,}000\ \text{bits}\). Transmission delay \(= \dfrac{\text{bits}}{\text{rate}} = \dfrac{12{,}000}{10 \times 10^{6}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s} = 1.2\ \text{ms}\).

front: A signal propagates at \(2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}\) along a \(300\ \text{km}\) link. Find the propagation delay.
explanation: Propagation delay \(= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} = \dfrac{300 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m}}{2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s} = 1.5\ \text{ms}\).

front: A link has bandwidth \(1\ \text{Mbps}\) and one-way propagation delay \(20\ \text{ms}\). Compute the bandwidth-delay product in bits.
explanation: Bandwidth-delay product \(= \text{bandwidth} \times \text{delay} = (1 \times 10^{6}\ \text{bits/s}) \times (20 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}) = 20{,}000\ \text{bits}\). This equals the number of bits in flight filling the link.

front: A \(5\ \text{MB}\) file (use \(1\ \text{MB} = 10^{6}\ \text{bytes}\)) is sent over a \(100\ \text{Mbps}\) link with one-way propagation delay \(10\ \text{ms}\). Find the total time for the last bit to arrive.
explanation: Bits: \(5 \times 10^{6} \times 8 = 4 \times 10^{7}\ \text{bits}\). Transmission time \(= \dfrac{4 \times 10^{7}}{100 \times 10^{6}} = 0.4\ \text{s}\). Total \(= 0.4 + 0.01 = 0.41\ \text{s}\).

front: A TCP connection has a maximum receive window of \(64\ \text{KiB}\) (\(65{,}536\) bytes) over a path with \(\text{RTT} = 40\ \text{ms}\). Estimate the maximum achievable throughput.
explanation: Throughput \(\approx \dfrac{\text{window}}{\text{RTT}} = \dfrac{65{,}536 \times 8\ \text{bits}}{40 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}} = \dfrac{524{,}288}{0.04} \approx 1.31 \times 10^{7}\ \text{bps} \approx 13.1\ \text{Mbps}\).

front: In a stop-and-wait ARQ link the frame transmission time is \(1\ \text{ms}\) and the one-way propagation delay is \(4\ \text{ms}\). Neglecting ACK and processing time, find the link utilization.
explanation: Utilization \(U = \dfrac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p} = \dfrac{1}{1 + 2(4)} = \dfrac{1}{9} \approx 0.111 = 11.1\%\).

front: A \(10\ \text{Mbps}\) link has \(\text{RTT} = 30\ \text{ms}\) and uses \(1250\)-byte frames. What minimum sliding-window size (in frames) is needed to fully utilize the link?
explanation: Frame transmission time \(T_t = \dfrac{1250 \times 8}{10 \times 10^{6}} = 1\ \text{ms}\). Full utilization needs \(W \ge 1 + \dfrac{\text{RTT}}{T_t} = 1 + \dfrac{30}{1} = 31\) frames.

front: A Go-Back-N protocol uses a sender window size of \(15\). What is the minimum number of bits required for the sequence-number field?
explanation: Go-Back-N requires the sequence-number space to satisfy \(2^{m} \ge W + 1\). With \(W = 15\): \(2^{m} \ge 16\), so \(m = 4\) bits (\(2^{4} = 16\)).

front: A noiseless channel has bandwidth \(3\ \text{kHz}\) and uses \(4\) signal levels. Using Nyquist's theorem, find the maximum data rate.
A channel has bandwidth \(4\ \text{kHz}\) and signal-to-noise ratio \(\text{SNR} = 1023\) (linear). Using the Shannon-Hartley theorem, find the channel capacity.
A telephone channel has bandwidth \(3.4\ \text{kHz}\) and \(\text{SNR} = 30\ \text{dB}\). Estimate the Shannon channel capacity.
explanation: Convert dB to linear: \(\text{SNR} = 10^{30/10} = 1000\). Then \(C = B\log_{2}(1 + \text{SNR}) = 3400\log_{2}(1001) \approx 3400 \times 9.97 \approx 33{,}900\ \text{bps} \approx 33.9\ \text{kbps}\).

front: A \(10\ \text{Mbps}\) link uses Manchester line encoding. What is the required signaling (baud) rate?
explanation: Manchester encoding places a transition in the middle of every bit, giving up to \(2\) signal elements per bit. Signal rate \(= 2 \times\) data rate \(= 2 \times 10\ \text{Mbps} = 20\ \text{Mbaud}\).

front: An IPv4 packet carries a TCP segment with a \(20\)-byte IPv4 header, a \(20\)-byte TCP header, and \(1460\) bytes of application data. What is the protocol efficiency (payload divided by total bytes)?
explanation: Total size \(= 20 + 20 + 1460 = 1500\ \text{bytes}\) (the typical Ethernet MTU). Efficiency \(= \dfrac{1460}{1500} \approx 0.973 = 97.3\%\).

front: In the TCP/IP model, the transport layer passes a segment down to the network layer. What is the resulting network-layer protocol data unit (PDU) called, and what does the network layer add to form it?
back: A packet (IP datagram); the network layer prepends an IP header containing source and destination IP addresses
explanation: Encapsulation adds a header at each layer. The transport-layer PDU is a segment; the network layer wraps it with an IP header (source/destination IP addresses, TTL, protocol, etc.) to form a packet (datagram); the data-link layer then adds its own header and trailer to form a frame.
